I've done some tests with UTF-8 strings, and think string formatting with precision doesn't work as expected.

`include/fmt/format.h`: `write_nonfinite()` restores the saved alignment and fill when specs use numeric alignment; if no alignment preceded the zero flag, it uses right alignment.

The latest edits have not been built or tested.
next_actions: Rebuild and rerun `ctest --test-dir /build --output-on-failure --no-tests=error -R '^format-test$'` against the latest edits.
Check that both nonfinite formatting tests pass and that `format_test.width` still passes; then run the full verification command if time permits.
rejected_approaches: The first `on_zero()` change applied zero-padding only when alignment was `none`; it was superseded because it discarded zero-padding for explicit numeric alignment such as `{:>06.0f}`.

which makes `is_formattable<std::tuple<T>>::value` true:
https://godbolt.org/z/G3zsT4q4W

even when the `T` is not formattable, and trying to format `std::tuple<T>` will lead to a hard error.

The protected CTest adapter builds and runs each regression target. Source /src; build /build. Run reproduce for F2P feedback."}

changes: Only include/fmt/ranges.h was edited. Current code adds detail::is_tuple_formattable_impl<TupleT, Char, N>, recursively checking each std::tuple_element with is_formattable and using N=0 as the true base case.
Tuple formatter SFINAE now uses detail::is_tuple_formattable<TupleT, Char>::value, guarded by fmt::is_tuple_like.
Current source hash: 5cb33873d41c47a8fbcd40ca4e11b3933f224c1266653d6c1f6d7726124982a7.
evidence_refs: Earlier compile-failure output: logs/11f3cdb15f814dc9bfb3e7012a7bcfb8/stdout.bin and logs/443e98800fea46e3b3299639b937f9ce/stdout.bin; full tool outputs: agent/tool-results/s000009.t01.json and agent/tool-results/s000010.t01.json.
findings: Baseline ranges-test failed because fmt::is_formattable<std::tuple<...>>::value was true for tuples containing unformattable elements; assertions are in test/ranges-test.cc:98-102.
The baseline had 23 of 24 ranges tests pass; the other listed P2P tests passed.
next_actions: Run `ctest --test-dir /build --output-on-failure --no-tests=error -R '^ranges-test$'` to build and verify the current edit; repair any failures, then run the full CTest suite if it passes.
rejected_approaches: The initial pack-expansion implementation specialized on index_sequence but produced incomplete-type errors.
Changing that specialization to integer_sequence still produced incomplete-type errors; both implementations were replaced by the current recursive implementation.
summary_state.task_and_scope: Fix tuple formattability detection in include/fmt/ranges.h. Base commit: 11e73853be14cf0994732a60b20f432bb35f1cc8.
visible_feedback: Baseline targeted CTest exited 8; four tuple formattability assertions reported Actual: true, Expected: false.

An early targeted CTest found no tests, and a build attempt reported “could not load cache”; CMake was then configured successfully. That configure emitted a warning that CMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM was unused.
The earlier pack-expansion trait attempts failed compilation with incomplete is_tuple_formattable_impl errors and downstream “Cannot format an argument” static assertions.
The latest recursive-trait edit has not been tested.

```
   replacement_field: "{" [`arg_id`] [":" (`format_spec` | `chrono_format_spec`)] "}"

   chrono_format_spec: [[`fill`]`align`][`width`]["." `precision`][`chrono_specs`]

   conversion_spec: "%" [`modifier`] `chrono_type`
```

suggests to me that `{:>30%H}` is valid, but this is not what fmt-9.1.0 and/or master @ b90895412f46e18e5b17efdea2c8f79e7d7504b3 outputs.

Input:

```c
#include <chrono>
#include <fmt/core.h>
#include <fmt/chrono.h>
int main()
{
        fmt::print("{:>30d}\n", 30);
        fmt::print("{:>30%H:%M}\n", std::chrono::system_clock::now());
}
```

Output:

```
                            30
>3023:48
```

Expected:

```
                            30
                         23:48

   conversion_spec: "%" [`modifier`] `chrono_type`
```

suggests to me that `{:>30%H}` is valid, but this is not what fmt-9.1.0 and/or master @ b90895412f46e18e5b17efdea2c8f79e7d7504b3 outputs.

```c
#include <chrono>

int main()

}

                            30
>3023:48

Expected:

```
                            30
                         23:48

overflow with std::chrono::time_point
`std::chrono::system_clock::time_point` on linux platforms uses nanosecond resolution and a 64 bit signed counter, hence is unable to represent dates beyond year 2262. This can be circumvented by using a custom `time_point` with a lower time resolution when doing time calculations, such as
```c++
using my_time_point = std::chrono::time_point<std::chrono::system_clock, std::chrono::milliseconds>;
```

Unfortunately, it seems that fmtlib is unable to correctly format such time points despite the lower time resolution. Here is an example that reproduces the problem:

```c++
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <fmt/chrono.h>

#if defined(__cpp_lib_format) && __cpp_lib_format >= 202106L
#define HAS_STD_FORMAT
#endif

#if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
#include <format>
#endif

int main() {
    std::cout << "fmt version: " << FMT_VERSION << "\n";

    using TimePointBad = std::chrono::system_clock::time_point;
    auto timeBad = TimePointBad{} + std::chrono::years{1030};
    std::cout << "bad time_point years:  " <<
        1970 + std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::years>(timeBad.time_since_epoch()).count() << "\n";
    std::cout << "fmt::format:           " << fmt::format("{:%F %T}", timeBad) << "\n";
    #if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
    std::cout << "std::format:           " << std::format("{:%F %T}", timeBad) << "\n";
    #else
    std::cout << "std::format:           not available\n";
    #endif

    using TimePointGood = std::chrono::time_point<std::chrono::system_clock, std::chrono::milliseconds>;
    auto timeGood = TimePointGood{} + std::chrono::years{1030};
    std::cout << "good time_point years: " <<
        1970 + std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::years>(timeGood.time_since_epoch()).count() << "\n";
    std::cout << "fmt::format:           " << fmt::format("{:%F %T}", timeGood) << "\n";
    #if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
    std::cout << "std::format:           " << std::format("{:%F %T}", timeGood) << "\n";
    #else
    std::cout << "std::format:           not available\n";
    #endif

    return 0;
}
```

Output from latest master commit on my system (Ubuntu GCC 11.4; doesn't have `<format>`):
```
fmt version: 100101
bad time_point years:  1831
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:52.580896768
std::format:           not available
good time_point years: 3000
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53.000
std::format:           not available
```

Output lines 2 and 3 show the problem of the standard `std::chrono::system_clock::time_point`; this is the output I expect.

Output line 5 shows that, using `TimePointGood` with millisecond resolution, the time point itself is able to represent dates far in the future.

Output line 6 shows that fmtlib still overflows.

[Godbolt link](https://godbolt.org/z/4MYETo4qo); this is running an older version of fmtlib but it also affected. Using gcc trunk with `std::format` shows that the standard `format` doesn't have the issue and outputs what one would expect:
```
fmt version: 90100
bad time_point years:  1831
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53
std::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:52.580896768
good time_point years: 3000
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53
std::format:           2999-12-31 18:36:00.000
```

overflow with std::chrono::time_point
`std::chrono::system_clock::time_point` on linux platforms uses nanosecond resolution and a 64 bit signed counter, hence is unable to represent dates beyond year 2262. This can be circumvented by using a custom `time_point` with a lower time resolution when doing time calculations, such as
```c++
using my_time_point = std::chrono::time_point<std::chrono::system_clock, std::chrono::milliseconds>;
```

Unfortunately, it seems that fmtlib is unable to correctly format such time points despite the lower time resolution. Here is an example that reproduces the problem:

```c++
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <fmt/chrono.h>

#if defined(__cpp_lib_format) && __cpp_lib_format >= 202106L
#define HAS_STD_FORMAT
#endif

#if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
#include <format>
#endif

int main() {
    std::cout << "fmt version: " << FMT_VERSION << "\n";

    using TimePointBad = std::chrono::system_clock::time_point;
    auto timeBad = TimePointBad{} + std::chrono::years{1030};
    std::cout << "bad time_point years:  " <<
        1970 + std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::years>(timeBad.time_since_epoch()).count() << "\n";
    std::cout << "fmt::format:           " << fmt::format("{:%F %T}", timeBad) << "\n";
    #if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
    std::cout << "std::format:           " << std::format("{:%F %T}", timeBad) << "\n";
    #else
    std::cout << "std::format:           not available\n";
    #endif

    using TimePointGood = std::chrono::time_point<std::chrono::system_clock, std::chrono::milliseconds>;
    auto timeGood = TimePointGood{} + std::chrono::years{1030};
    std::cout << "good time_point years: " <<
        1970 + std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::years>(timeGood.time_since_epoch()).count() << "\n";
    std::cout << "fmt::format:           " << fmt::format("{:%F %T}", timeGood) << "\n";
    #if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
    std::cout << "std::format:           " << std::format("{:%F %T}", timeGood) << "\n";
    #else
    std::cout << "std::format:           not available\n";
    #endif

    return 0;
}
```

Output from latest master commit on my system (Ubuntu GCC 11.4; doesn't have `<format>`):
```
fmt version: 100101
bad time_point years:  1831
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:52.580896768
std::format:           not available
good time_point years: 3000
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53.000
std::format:           not available
```

Output lines 2 and 3 show the problem of the standard `std::chrono::system_clock::time_point`; this is the output I expect.

Output line 5 shows that, using `TimePointGood` with millisecond resolution, the time point itself is able to represent dates far in the future.

Output line 6 shows that fmtlib still overflows.

[Godbolt link](https://godbolt.org/z/4MYETo4qo); this is running an older version of fmtlib but it also affected. Using gcc trunk with `std::format` shows that the standard `format` doesn't have the issue and outputs what one would expect:
```
fmt version: 90100
bad time_point years:  1831
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53
std::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:52.580896768
good time_point years: 3000
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53
std::format:           2999-12-31 18:36:00.000
```

overflow with std::chrono::time_point
`std::chrono::system_clock::time_point` on linux platforms uses nanosecond resolution and a 64 bit signed counter, hence is unable to represent dates beyond year 2262. This can be circumvented by using a custom `time_point` with a lower time resolution when doing time calculations, such as
```c++
using my_time_point = std::chrono::time_point<std::chrono::system_clock, std::chrono::milliseconds>;
```

Unfortunately, it seems that fmtlib is unable to correctly format such time points despite the lower time resolution. Here is an example that reproduces the problem:

```c++
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <fmt/chrono.h>

#if defined(__cpp_lib_format) && __cpp_lib_format >= 202106L
#define HAS_STD_FORMAT
#endif

#if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
#include <format>
#endif

int main() {
    std::cout << "fmt version: " << FMT_VERSION << "\n";

    using TimePointBad = std::chrono::system_clock::time_point;
    auto timeBad = TimePointBad{} + std::chrono::years{1030};
    std::cout << "bad time_point years:  " <<
        1970 + std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::years>(timeBad.time_since_epoch()).count() << "\n";
    std::cout << "fmt::format:           " << fmt::format("{:%F %T}", timeBad) << "\n";
    #if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
    std::cout << "std::format:           " << std::format("{:%F %T}", timeBad) << "\n";
    #else
    std::cout << "std::format:           not available\n";
    #endif

    using TimePointGood = std::chrono::time_point<std::chrono::system_clock, std::chrono::milliseconds>;
    auto timeGood = TimePointGood{} + std::chrono::years{1030};
    std::cout << "good time_point years: " <<
        1970 + std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::years>(timeGood.time_since_epoch()).count() << "\n";
    std::cout << "fmt::format:           " << fmt::format("{:%F %T}", timeGood) << "\n";
    #if defined(HAS_STD_FORMAT)
    std::cout << "std::format:           " << std::format("{:%F %T}", timeGood) << "\n";
    #else
    std::cout << "std::format:           not available\n";
    #endif

    return 0;
}
```

Output from latest master commit on my system (Ubuntu GCC 11.4; doesn't have `<format>`):
```
fmt version: 100101
bad time_point years:  1831
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:52.580896768
std::format:           not available
good time_point years: 3000
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53.000
std::format:           not available
```

Output lines 2 and 3 show the problem of the standard `std::chrono::system_clock::time_point`; this is the output I expect.

Output line 5 shows that, using `TimePointGood` with millisecond resolution, the time point itself is able to represent dates far in the future.

Output line 6 shows that fmtlib still overflows.

[Godbolt link](https://godbolt.org/z/4MYETo4qo); this is running an older version of fmtlib but it also affected. Using gcc trunk with `std::format` shows that the standard `format` doesn't have the issue and outputs what one would expect:
```
fmt version: 90100
bad time_point years:  1831
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53
std::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:52.580896768
good time_point years: 3000
fmt::format:           1830-11-22 19:26:53
std::format:           2999-12-31 18:36:00.000
```

```
int main() {
    const auto x = 123456789;
    std::clog << std::format("{:LX}", x) << ' ' << fmt::format("{:LX}", x);
}
```

changes: Edited only `include/fmt/format.h`: `loc_writer` now dispatches decimal, hexadecimal, binary, and octal presentations; added `write_base` to format and locale-group non-decimal digits while preserving sign/alternate prefixes and uppercase hex.
Changed source SHA-256: `c1f64a2444ab3bd4748f08868e2295e54a825fdc75aa0a69c722c4c7ff1cc86e`.
findings: The baseline `loc_writer::operator()(T)` in `include/fmt/format.h` grouped integers as decimal without checking `specs.type`, causing localized `x`, `b`, and `o` formats to produce decimal digits.
Baseline `format_test.format_locale` failed three assertions; the other 119 tests in `format-test` passed. Baseline evidence: `logs/2dbee5bc69fb472c8062c36d32d7c41b/stdout.bin`.
next_actions: Run the full CTest suite with `ctest --test-dir /build --output-on-failure --no-tests=error`.
Consider adding regression coverage for localized uppercase radix forms and relevant format-spec combinations.
summary_state.task_and_scope: Fix localized integer formatting in {fmt}: radix type specifiers such as hex, binary, and octal should not be rendered as decimal. Baseline commit: a2d4156f57d04e5ad843ac7ef9f5607b50781751.
visible_feedback: CMake configure and full build succeeded (command `cb2b6f0ca0cb4d02aef3cc940bb1c38e`, exit 0).

of floating-point numbers is incorrect if the output is localized and the integer part is zero
Consider the following code (https://godbolt.org/z/f7czaGcdG):
```
#include <locale>
#include <fmt/printf.h>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    std::locale::global(std::locale("en_US.UTF-8"));

    fmt::print("     X = {:19.3Lf}\n", -119.921);
    fmt::print("     Y = {:19.3Lf}\n", 2'194.139);
    fmt::print("     Z = {:19.3Lf}\n", -57.639);
    fmt::print("    VX = {:19.3Lf}\n", -5.980);
    fmt::print("    VY = {:19.3Lf}\n", -2.119);
    fmt::print("    VZ = {:19.3Lf}\n", 0.295);
}
```
The last number will be misaligned in the output:
```
     X =           -119.921
     Y =          2,194.139
     Z =            -57.639
    VX =             -5.980
    VY =             -2.119
    VZ =               0.295

Consider the following code (https://godbolt.org/z/f7czaGcdG):
```
#include <locale>
#include <fmt/printf.h>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    std::locale::global(std::locale("en_US.UTF-8"));

    fmt::print("     X = {:19.3Lf}\n", -119.921);
    fmt::print("     Y = {:19.3Lf}\n", 2'194.139);
    fmt::print("     Z = {:19.3Lf}\n", -57.639);
    fmt::print("    VX = {:19.3Lf}\n", -5.980);
    fmt::print("    VY = {:19.3Lf}\n", -2.119);
    fmt::print("    VZ = {:19.3Lf}\n", 0.295);
}
```
The last number will be misaligned in the output:
```
     X =           -119.921
     Y =          2,194.139
     Z =            -57.639
    VX =             -5.980
    VY =             -2.119
    VZ =               0.295
```
If you change the last number to `1.295`, the alignment will be correct. It is also correct if you remove `L`.

Consider the following code (https://godbolt.org/z/f7czaGcdG):
```
#include <locale>
#include <fmt/printf.h>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    std::locale::global(std::locale("en_US.UTF-8"));

    fmt::print("     X = {:19.3Lf}\n", -119.921);
    fmt::print("     Y = {:19.3Lf}\n", 2'194.139);
    fmt::print("     Z = {:19.3Lf}\n", -57.639);
    fmt::print("    VX = {:19.3Lf}\n", -5.980);
    fmt::print("    VY = {:19.3Lf}\n", -2.119);
    fmt::print("    VZ = {:19.3Lf}\n", 0.295);
}
```
The last number will be misaligned in the output:
```
     X =           -119.921
     Y =          2,194.139
     Z =            -57.639
    VX =             -5.980
    VY =             -2.119
    VZ =               0.295
```
If you change the last number to `1.295`, the alignment will be correct. It is also correct if you remove `L`.

The protected CTest adapter builds and runs each regression target. Source /src; build /build. Run reproduce for F2P feedback."}

uses wrong overload when formatting to memory_buffer with a text_style
Hi, I encountered an issue when attempting to format a styled message to a memory buffer. Instead of calling the overload from color.h, the overload from format.h is used, causing a compile error. This only occurs when formatting to fmt::memory_buffer (output iterators work perfectly).
Example:
```c++
// fails
fmt::memory_buffer buf;
fmt::format_to(buf, fmt::emphasis::bold, "Hello, {}!", "world");

// works fine
std::string str;
fmt::format_to(std::back_inserter(str), fmt::emphasis::bold, "Hello, {}!", "world");
```

The protected CTest adapter builds and runs each regression target. Source /src; build /build. Run reproduce for F2P feedback."}

seconds precision does not match C++20 spec
According to https://eel.is/c++draft/time.format#tab:time.format.spec, under the `%S` specifier:

> If the precision of the input cannot be exactly represented with seconds, then the format is a decimal floating-point number with a fixed format and a precision matching that of the precision of the input (or to a microseconds precision if the conversion to floating-point decimal seconds cannot be made within 18 fractional digits).

When outputting a `std::chrono::system_clock::time_point` (with resolution in nanoseconds) via the `%S` format specifier, fmt currently only prints the whole seconds, and does not add the decimal fraction according to the C++20 spec.

Godbolt demo: https://godbolt.org/z/h4rfo5zTr

It outputs `01`, where it should be `01.234000000` according to the spec.

Using [hinnant/date](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date), I get the expected result:
```c++
    using time_type = typename std::chrono::system_clock::time_point;
    time_type t{std::chrono::milliseconds{1234}};
    auto s = date::format(std::locale::classic(), "%S", t);
    fmt::print("{}\n", s); // prints 01.234000000
```

If one wants to print whole seconds with a `system_clock::time_point`, they first have to [floor](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/time_point/floor) it to a `sys_time<std::chrono::seconds>`.

This problem also affects the `%T` specifier.

```
template <typename... Args>
void error(fmt::format_string<Args...> fmt_str, Args&&... args) {
    const fmt::text_style ts = fmt::emphasis::bold | fg(fmt::color::red);
    fmt::print(stderr, ts, "ERROR: ");
    fmt::print(stderr, ts, fmt_str, std::forward<Args>(args)...);
    fmt::print(stderr, "\n");
}
```

I was writing a forwarding wrapper around fmt, something like this (prints "ERROR: " and makes the text red):

```
template <typename... Args>
void error(fmt::format_string<Args...> fmt_str, Args&&... args) {
    const fmt::text_style ts = fmt::emphasis::bold | fg(fmt::color::red);
    fmt::print(stderr, ts, "ERROR: ");
    fmt::print(stderr, ts, fmt_str, std::forward<Args>(args)...);
    fmt::print(stderr, "\n");
}
```

That results in the following errors:

```
In file included from common/logging_test.cc:2:
./common/logging.h:28:5: error: no matching function for call to 'print'
    fmt::print(stderr, ts, fmt_str, std::forward<Args>(args)...);
    ^~~~~~~~~~
common/logging_test.cc:35:33: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'error<int>' requested here
          EXPECT_NO_MEMORY_ALLOCATIONS(error("foo {}", 42));
                                       ^
external/com_github_fmtlib_fmt/include/fmt/core.h:3293:17: note: candidate function [with T = <const fmt::text_style &, fmt::basic_format_string<char, int> &, int>] not viable: no known conversion from 'FILE *' (aka '_IO_FILE *') to 'format_string<const fmt::text_style &, fmt::basic_format_string<char, int> &, int>' (aka 'basic_format_string<char, const fmt::text_style &, fmt::basic_format_string<char, int> &, int>') for 1st argument
FMT_INLINE void print(format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args) {
                ^
external/com_github_fmtlib_fmt/include/fmt/core.h:3310:17: note: candidate function [with T = <fmt::basic_format_string<char, int> &, int>] not viable: no known conversion from 'const fmt::text_style' to 'format_string<fmt::basic_format_string<char, int> &, int>' (aka 'basic_format_string<char, fmt::basic_format_string<char, int> &, int>') for 2nd argument
FMT_INLINE void print(std::FILE* f, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args) {
                ^
external/com_github_fmtlib_fmt/include/fmt/color.h:508:6: note: candidate template ignored: requirement 'detail::is_string<fmt::basic_format_string<char, int>>::value' was not satisfied [with S = fmt::basic_format_string<char, int>, Args = <int>]
void print(std::FILE* f, const text_style& ts, const S& format_str,
     ^
external/com_github_fmtlib_fmt/include/fmt/color.h:527:6: note: candidate template ignored: requirement 'detail::is_string<fmt::text_style>::value' was not satisfied [with S = fmt::text_style, Args = <fmt::basic_format_string<char, int>, int>]
void print(const text_style& ts, const S& format_str, const Args&... args) {
     ^
```

The failure comes from the fact that the targeted overload (3rd candidate in the above error messages, taking `FILE*`, `const text_style&` and `const S&`) is ignored (by Sfinae) because `fmt::basic_format_string` is not a string (as checked by `detail::is_string`).

I can easily fix this in my code with an explicit conversion to string_view, with `static_cast<fmt::string_view>(fmt_str)`, but it seems like this should be supported, and that it would be an easy fix by just letting `basic_format_string` pass the `detail::is_string` test, unless there is some unintended side-effect I can't see.

`c` accepted in combination with `bool`
While applying massive random tests with generated format-specs, it turned out that the `c` presentation-type is allowed for `bool`. 

```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#9c}"}; // invalid format string
    std::cout << fmt::format(formatString, false) << std::endl; // accepted, compile error expected
    std::cout << std::format(formatString, false) << std::endl; // rejected, compiler error as expected
```

[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/xzbsdq49o)

While writing for `false` the value is missing
```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#2c}"};
    auto const s1{fmt::format(formatString, false)};
    std::cout << s1 << std::endl; // prints "X"
```
[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/ccz388zMr)

for `true` the output seems to include uninitialized memory (unprintable chars)
```cpp

`c` accepted in combination with `bool`
While applying massive random tests with generated format-specs, it turned out that the `c` presentation-type is allowed for `bool`. 

```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#9c}"}; // invalid format string
    std::cout << fmt::format(formatString, false) << std::endl; // accepted, compile error expected
    std::cout << std::format(formatString, false) << std::endl; // rejected, compiler error as expected
```

[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/xzbsdq49o)

While writing for `false` the value is missing
```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#2c}"};
    auto const s1{fmt::format(formatString, false)};
    std::cout << s1 << std::endl; // prints "X"
```
[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/ccz388zMr)

for `true` the output seems to include uninitialized memory (unprintable chars)
```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#2c}"};
    auto const s1{fmt::format(formatString, false)};
    std::cout << s1 << std::endl; // prints "?X", where ? is an unprintable char
```
[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/W5dGjK5h9)

`c` accepted in combination with `bool`
While applying massive random tests with generated format-specs, it turned out that the `c` presentation-type is allowed for `bool`. 

```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#9c}"}; // invalid format string
    std::cout << fmt::format(formatString, false) << std::endl; // accepted, compile error expected
    std::cout << std::format(formatString, false) << std::endl; // rejected, compiler error as expected
```

[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/xzbsdq49o)

While writing for `false` the value is missing
```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#2c}"};
    auto const s1{fmt::format(formatString, false)};
    std::cout << s1 << std::endl; // prints "X"
```
[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/ccz388zMr)

for `true` the output seems to include uninitialized memory (unprintable chars)
```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#2c}"};
    auto const s1{fmt::format(formatString, false)};
    std::cout << s1 << std::endl; // prints "?X", where ? is an unprintable char
```
[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/W5dGjK5h9)

While applying massive random tests with generated format-specs, it turned out that the `c` presentation-type is allowed for `bool`. 

```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#9c}"}; // invalid format string
    std::cout << fmt::format(formatString, false) << std::endl; // accepted, compile error expected
    std::cout << std::format(formatString, false) << std::endl; // rejected, compiler error as expected
```

[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/xzbsdq49o)

While writing for `false` the value is missing
```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#2c}"};
    auto const s1{fmt::format(formatString, false)};
    std::cout << s1 << std::endl; // prints "X"
```
[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/ccz388zMr)

for `true` the output seems to include uninitialized memory (unprintable chars)
```cpp
    std::string_view constexpr formatString{"{:X<#2c}"};
    auto const s1{fmt::format(formatString, false)};
    std::cout << s1 << std::endl; // prints "?X", where ? is an unprintable char
```
[godbolt](https://www.godbolt.org/z/W5dGjK5h9)

#include <fmt/args.h>

summary_state.task_and_scope: Fix incorrect automatic positional indexing when `dynamic_format_arg_store` arguments mix named and unnamed values; issue also mentions `vformat` and `vprint`. Work is in `/src`.
findings: `dynamic_format_arg_store` stores a metadata placeholder alongside named values, while named argument IDs refer to positions in the argument array.
Existing `args_test.reserve` expects automatic indexing in a dynamic store to select unnamed arguments, not named ones.
changes: `include/fmt/base.h`: added `is_dynamic_args_bit` and `basic_format_args::get_positional_arg_id(int)` to map automatic indices past named entries for dynamic stores; updated `max_size()` to exclude descriptor control bits.

`include/fmt/format.h`: changed runtime `format_handler::on_arg_id()` to translate automatic IDs through `context.args().get_positional_arg_id(...)`; explicit numeric IDs and named lookups remain unchanged.
`include/fmt/args.h`: `get_types()` now sets the dynamic-store bit and reports the argument count without the named-metadata placeholder.
No test files were edited; the existing named/automatic regression test is in `test/args-test.cc`.
visible_feedback: CMake configure and build of `args-test` succeeded.
An intermediate, since-revised attempt failed `args_test.reserve`: expected `42 and 1.5`, got `42 and 42`.
The latest changes that add dynamic-store-specific positional mapping have not been tested in the visible conversation.
rejected_approaches: A first attempt advanced automatic indexing globally whenever a named field appeared. It was reverted because it conflicted with dynamic-store behavior and did not preserve the expected `reserve` result.
Counting the named-metadata placeholder as an argument was inconsistent with positional indexing; the latest `get_types()` edit excludes it.
next_actions: Rebuild and rerun the focused test: `cmake --build /build --target args-test -j2 && ctest --test-dir /build --output-on-failure -R '^args-test$'`.
If it passes, verify the reported `vformat` reproduction and check `vprint` plus relevant mixed named/positional edge cases.

vformat & vprint functions produce incorrect output when mixing named and positional arguments.
When using the dynamic_format_arg_store with both named and positional args on fmt, the output produced is incorrect.

A minimal reproduction of the issue is shown in the snippet below:

<details>

<summary>A minimal reproduction of the issue is shown in the snippet below:</summary>

```cpp
#include <fmt/args.h>
#include <fmt/core.h>

int main() {
    fmt::dynamic_format_arg_store<fmt::format_context> store;
    store.push_back(1);
    store.push_back(fmt::arg("b", 2));
    store.push_back(3);

    // Prints 1 2 2 instead of 1 2 3
    fmt::vprint("{} {b} {}", store);
}
```

</details>

changes: `include/fmt/base.h`: added `basic_format_parse_context::check_arg_id(basic_string_view<Char>, int id)` to advance automatic indexing past a named argument's resolved ID when appropriate; `format_string_checker::on_arg_id(name)` now calls it.
`include/fmt/format.h`: `format_handler::on_arg_id(name)` now passes the resolved `arg_id` to the parse context after checking that the name exists.

findings: Baseline `args_test.named_with_automatic_index` failed: expected `1 2 3 4`, got `1 2 3 2` (the final automatic field reused argument index 1).

rejected_approaches: Advancing the automatic index for every named field made `args_test.reserve` fail: expected `42 and 1.5`, got `42 and 42`. The final logic uses the resolved named-argument ID and current cursor.

According to https://eel.is/c++draft/time.format#tab:time.format.spec, under the `%S` specifier:

> If the precision of the input cannot be exactly represented with seconds, then the format is a decimal floating-point number with a fixed format and a precision matching that of the precision of the input (or to a microseconds precision if the conversion to floating-point decimal seconds cannot be made within 18 fractional digits).

When outputting a `std::chrono::system_clock::time_point` (with resolution in nanoseconds) via the `%S` format specifier, fmt currently only prints the whole seconds, and does not add the decimal fraction according to the C++20 spec.

Godbolt demo: https://godbolt.org/z/h4rfo5zTr

It outputs `01`, where it should be `01.234000000` according to the spec.

Using [hinnant/date](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date), I get the expected result:
```c++
    using time_type = typename std::chrono::system_clock::time_point;
    time_type t{std::chrono::milliseconds{1234}};
    auto s = date::format(std::locale::classic(), "%S", t);
    fmt::print("{}\n", s); // prints 01.234000000
```

If one wants to print whole seconds with a `system_clock::time_point`, they first have to [floor](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/time_point/floor) it to a `sys_time<std::chrono::seconds>`.

This problem also affects the `%T` specifier.

seconds precision does not match C++20 spec
According to https://eel.is/c++draft/time.format#tab:time.format.spec, under the `%S` specifier:

> If the precision of the input cannot be exactly represented with seconds, then the format is a decimal floating-point number with a fixed format and a precision matching that of the precision of the input (or to a microseconds precision if the conversion to floating-point decimal seconds cannot be made within 18 fractional digits).

When outputting a `std::chrono::system_clock::time_point` (with resolution in nanoseconds) via the `%S` format specifier, fmt currently only prints the whole seconds, and does not add the decimal fraction according to the C++20 spec.

Godbolt demo: https://godbolt.org/z/h4rfo5zTr

It outputs `01`, where it should be `01.234000000` according to the spec.

Using [hinnant/date](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date), I get the expected result:
```c++
    using time_type = typename std::chrono::system_clock::time_point;
    time_type t{std::chrono::milliseconds{1234}};
    auto s = date::format(std::locale::classic(), "%S", t);
    fmt::print("{}\n", s); // prints 01.234000000
```

If one wants to print whole seconds with a `system_clock::time_point`, they first have to [floor](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/time_point/floor) it to a `sys_time<std::chrono::seconds>`.

This problem also affects the `%T` specifier.

The protected CTest adapter builds and runs each regression target. Source /src; build /build. Run reproduce for F2P feedback."}

changes: Edited only `include/fmt/chrono.h`; current source tree SHA-256 is `30525f180de1a2debaf6d519b0c64bee88ddcc96558ddbeeedf20929322659d2`.
Changed the system-clock time-point formatter to delegate to `detail::format_time_point` and added `fractional_second_precision`, `write_fractional_seconds`, and `format_tm_specs` helpers.

`format_time_point` scans chrono format specs, formats `%S` and `%T` through the `std::tm` formatter, then appends fractional digits based on the duration period. This edit has not been built or tested.
findings: Baseline configure and build succeeded. Baseline `chrono-test` failed only `chrono_test.time_point` at `test/chrono-test.cc:106`: expected `"01.023"` for `{:%S}` on a millisecond-resolution time point, got `"01"` (23/24 tests passed).

The existing system-clock time-point formatter converts to `std::tm`/`strftime`, losing subsecond precision. The task also reports nanosecond-resolution `%S` should produce `01.234000000`; `%T` is affected too.
next_actions: Build the current edit, then rerun the targeted `chrono-test` through CTest; repair any compile or runtime failures.

Add or verify coverage for `%S` and `%T` with millisecond and nanosecond time points, including zero fractional values. Current `write_fractional_seconds` returns without emitting a fraction when the fraction is zero, even when the duration period implies fractional precision.
rejected_approaches: No code design was explicitly rejected in the visible conversation.
summary_state.task_and_scope: Implement C++20 fractional seconds for `std::chrono::system_clock::time_point` formatting with `%S`, and account for the reported impact on `%T`. Repository source is `/src`; baseline commit is `a8f51a04083ef9e4a81de5c0c8fcb9a13c2076be`.

Currently `fmt::format("{}", 0.1f)` with grisu produces `0.10000000149011612` (as would have been expected from `double(0.1f)`) rather than `0.1`.

Single precision formatting differs from double precision only in the calculation of the boundaries: https://github.com/google/double-conversion/blob/v3.1.5/double-conversion/fast-dtoa.cc#L525-L536

The protected CTest adapter builds and runs each regression target. Source /src; build /build. Run reproduce for F2P feedback."}

changes: `include/fmt/format-inl.h`: added `fp::compute_float_boundaries`; enabled `grisu_format` for types up to `uint64_t`, selected float-specific boundaries, and converted to `double` for `fp` construction and fallback.
`include/fmt/format.h`: updated `grisu_format` declarations for types up to `uint64_t` and passed the original float into Grisu from `write_fp`.
`src/format.cc`: added explicit float `grisu_format` instantiation.
Current source hash: `76b3af4eb8feb084acf843d8ee06d7a007c7f9482634bef5f18838c974d36783`.
findings: Baseline `format-impl-test` failed to compile because `fp` lacked `compute_float_boundaries`; `grisu-test` failed because formatting `0.1f` exposed its double-converted value.
After the edits, targeted `format-impl-test` and `grisu-test` passed.

A supplementary randomized float check still finds a possible shortest-formatting issue: bit pattern `0x4f4c6011` formats as `3428847872.0`, exceeding the check’s 9-significant-digit limit, though its round-trip check passed. The check’s initial digit count mistakenly included exponent digits; it was corrected to exclude them.
next_actions: Investigate and repair float boundary/shortest-digit behavior for cases such as `0x4f4c6011`; add focused regression coverage.
Rerun the randomized round-trip and significant-digit checks, then run full CTest verification.
rejected_approaches: `rg` was unavailable (`command not found`); subsequent searches used `grep`.
An initial CTest/build attempt after editing found no configured tests/cache. Reconfiguring `/build` resolved this.
The first randomized digit-count check included exponent digits and was corrected; its result was not treated as a valid shortestness failure.

visible_feedback: `format-impl-test` passed after reconfiguration (command `4644cba1933049bbb107d39bcf3f0f4a`).
`grisu-test` passed (command `16800b44eace428588a6607e2b487e60`).

According to https://eel.is/c++draft/time.format#tab:time.format.spec, under the `%S` specifier:

> If the precision of the input cannot be exactly represented with seconds, then the format is a decimal floating-point number with a fixed format and a precision matching that of the precision of the input (or to a microseconds precision if the conversion to floating-point decimal seconds cannot be made within 18 fractional digits).

It outputs `01`, where it should be `01.234000000` according to the spec.

Using [hinnant/date](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date), I get the expected result:
```c++

    time_type t{std::chrono::milliseconds{1234}};
    auto s = date::format(std::locale::classic(), "%S", t);
    fmt::print("{}\n", s); // prints 01.234000000
```

If one wants to print whole seconds with a `system_clock::time_point`, they first have to [floor](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/time_point/floor) it to a `sys_time<std::chrono::seconds>`.
